--- title: "Introduction to Inferential Statistics" author: "Yi Lu" date: "2026/11/11" format: html: embed-resources: true editor: visual --- ## Example 1: NJ happiness Suppose you conduct a survey of adults in New Jersey and ask each respondent to rate their happiness on a scale from 0 to 100. The following map shows the average happiness score for each county. What conclusions can you draw? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: :::
What's the truth Any pattern you see is actually **due to random chance**. The happiness score is randomly generated for each of the 21 counties using the *same* underlying distribution (**rnorm(21,mean=60,sd=15)**).
## Example 2: US crime rates This map is based on the [USArrests](USArrests_doc.html) dataset. What conclusions can you draw? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Murder Assault UrbanPop Rape Alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 Alaska 10.0 263 48 44.5 Arizona 8.1 294 80 31.0 Arkansas 8.8 190 50 19.5 California 9.0 276 91 40.6 Colorado 7.9 204 78 38.7 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: :::
What's the truth Unknown. Any pattern you see can be due to random chance, or can be statistically significant.
## Pattern you see in the data can be due to random chance! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sample(c('Success','Fail'),size=50,replace=T) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Fail" "Fail" "Fail" "Success" "Success" "Fail" "Success" [8] "Fail" "Fail" "Success" "Success" "Success" "Fail" "Fail" [15] "Success" "Fail" "Fail" "Fail" "Success" "Fail" "Success" [22] "Fail" "Fail" "Success" "Fail" "Success" "Success" "Success" [29] "Success" "Success" "Fail" "Fail" "Fail" "Fail" "Success" [36] "Success" "Success" "Success" "Fail" "Success" "Success" "Fail" [43] "Success" "Fail" "Fail" "Fail" "Success" "Success" "Success" [50] "Fail" ``` ::: ::: We see streaks of Fails and Successes, but these are all due to random chance!


## Inferential statistics We have been working with many different data and can describe the data in many ways (summary statistics, visualizations, correlations, etc.). However, **data does NOT equal to the truth!** - In any survey data: respondents are only a random sample of the population. If we see that, for instance, 23% of **respondents** in the `child.care` dataset used childcare, it does not mean that exactly 23% of the entire U.S. population used childcare. - In an NBA example: a player's *true* ability (of shooting field goals, for instance) is a **latent variable** that cannot be directly measured. For instance, in the 2024 NBA season, Mikal Bridges has a higher field goal percentage than Jalen Green, but it doesn't necessarily mean that Mikal Bridges is better than Jalen Green; maybe he is just lucky (i.e., his success is "due to random chance"). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(Lock5Data) NBAPlayers2024 %>% filter(Starts > 80, MinPerGame > 30 ) %>% select(Player, Pos, Team, Games, FGAttempt, FGMade, FGPct) %>% arrange(desc(Team)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Player Pos Team Games FGAttempt FGMade FGPct 1 Domantas Sabonis C SAC 82 1068 634 0.594 2 Jalen Green SG HOU 82 1332 563 0.423 3 Michael Porter Jr. SF DEN 81 1079 522 0.484 4 Mikal Bridges SF BRK 82 1294 564 0.436 ``` ::: ::: - Another way to think about this: most of the time, *data is not reproducible*: if I conduct the same survey again with different respondents, I will get a different percentage of respondents using childcare; Mikal Bridges is better than Jalen Green in 2024, but it is not a guarantee that he will also be better in 2025. ## p-value and statistical significance - **Descriptive statistics**, also referred to as Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), is about describing the *data* - **Inferential statistics** is about generalizing the conclusion to the *entire population* and/or the *truth* - Typically, a "hypothesis test" is conducted and a **p-value** is obtained - If p-value is large (\>0.05): the conclusion is *not* significant and due to random chance - If p-value is small (\<0.05): the conclusion is statistically significant - Definition of p-value: the probability of observing the data (i.e., test statistic) as extreme, or more extreme, than the one obtained, assuming the null hypothesis is true. ## Example 3: drug effect on tumor size Suppose a new drug is developed to treat a certain type of cancer and has been tested on 20 patients. Is the drug effective? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tumsize1 tumsize2 patient 1 15.454042 6.926204 patient 1 2 7.286632 14.213477 patient 2 3 11.628681 11.079898 patient 3 4 14.428575 10.482909 patient 4 5 9.524580 9.125362 patient 5 6 11.471811 9.149994 patient 6 7 9.493480 9.774322 patient 7 8 5.206460 10.899869 patient 8 9 10.554134 10.676206 patient 9 10 16.671018 9.649528 patient 10 11 15.437937 8.548358 patient 11 12 10.478542 10.441172 patient 12 13 14.385787 10.130264 patient 13 14 10.809951 9.408377 patient 14 15 7.876401 12.626095 patient 15 16 12.141398 8.267080 patient 16 17 11.616720 6.881314 patient 17 18 9.512484 8.905779 patient 18 19 11.369541 14.949419 patient 19 20 12.846685 9.973217 patient 20 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: Remember, the data alone does not tell us whether the drug is effective; we need to evaluate the statistical significance. We decide to conduct a **paired samples t-test**. What is the conclusion here? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(df.drug$tumsize1, df.drug$tumsize2, paired = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Paired t-test data: df.drug$tumsize1 and df.drug$tumsize2 t = 1.3812, df = 19, p-value = 0.1833 alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -0.6722583 3.2808597 sample estimates: mean difference 1.304301 ``` ::: :::
Solution The p-value is large (0.1833 \> 0.05), so we conclude that the drug is not statistically significant in reducing tumor size.
What's the truth Any pattern you see is indeed due to random chance. The tumor sizes before and after taking the drug are both randomly, and independently generated for each patient using the *same* underlying distribution (**rgamma(20,shape=20,rate=2)**).


## Intuition behind p-value: a thought experiment Suppose your data looks like this: Matt, he is wearing a blue t-shirt, a pair of jeans, some sneakers, sunglasses, and a baseball cap. He is holding his phone and listening to music on his headphones. Question: which scenario is more likely? - A: Matt is about to run a race. - B: Matt is not about to run a race.
Key idea IF Matt is about to run a race, what **should** he look like? In other words, IF scenario A is true, what **should** your data look like? This is called a **reference distribution**. **Reference distribution** ![Runners at the [2026 NYC marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_York_City_Marathon)](NYC2026.jpg) If your data is very "unusual" or "extreme" compared to the reference distribution, you would **reject** scenario A on the basis of your data. If not, i.e., your data looks pretty "likely" under the reference distribution, you would **fail to reject** scenario A. How likely is your data under the reference distribution? This is essentially what the **p-value** measures! Hence: **small** p-value -> **unlikely** data -> reject the null hypothesis (scenario A).
Question: if you decide scenario B is more likely, did you **prove** with certainty that Matt is not about to run a race?
Key idea No, you cannot **prove** that Matt is not about to run a race. You are just saying that the evidence is very strong against scenario A, meaning that your data is very unlikely under scenario A (i.e., it's unlikely that Matt would wear jeans to a race).
## Example 1: NJ happiness revisited Consider two scenarios: - A: every county in NJ is equally happy, on average. - B: Morris county is more happy than all of the other counties. You conduct your survey and look at your data (e.g., generate a map that looks like example 1), but how do you decide between scenario A and B? Key idea: if **scenario A** is true, what **should** your data look like?
Reference distribution under scenario A ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
Now, if your data looks like this, would you **reject** scenario A? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=30%} ::: ::: What if your data looks like this? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=30%} ::: ::: ## Example 3: drug effect revisited In the drug effect example, we can summarize the data by calculating the **mean difference** between the tumor sizes before and after treatment. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} df.drug$tumsize1 - df.drug$tumsize2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -6.92684415 -5.69340873 -4.74969350 -3.57987817 -0.28084238 -0.12207213 [7] 0.03736942 0.39921770 0.54878326 0.60670441 1.40157402 2.32181729 [13] 2.87346764 3.87431781 3.94566519 4.25552209 4.73540607 6.88957946 [19] 7.02148980 8.52783842 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(df.drug$tumsize1 - df.drug$tumsize2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.304301 ``` ::: ::: We need to decide between: - Scenario A: The drug has no effect (the null hypothesis) - Scenario B: The drug has an effect (the alternative hypothesis) Reference distribution: what **should** the mean difference look like **if the drug has no effect**? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Intro_to_Inferential_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: (This reference distribution is a t-distribution, that's why it's called a paired samples **t-test**. The derivation is based on the Central Limit Theorem.) Is our observed value (1.3) very extreme? What would you conclude?
